L749: # Plugins
L756: ## Overview
L757: 
L758: Plugins bundle capabilities into reusable workflows in ChatGPT and Codex. They can include skills, connectors, or both. Both products use one universal plugin directory, so the same public plugins are discoverable from their supported surfaces.
L759: 
L760: Plugins are available with ChatGPT Work on the web and with ChatGPT Work or Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app. Codex CLI also has a plugin browser for Codex environments. Plugins aren’t available in Chat, the IDE extension, or mobile.
L761: In the ChatGPT desktop app, select ChatGPT and turn on Work in the switcher, or select Codex. Then open Plugins to browse, install, and use plugins. Installed plugins can add skills, connectors, and MCP tools to new chats.
L762: 
L763: In ChatGPT web, turn on Work in the switcher and open Plugins to browse, install, and use plugins. A plugin can prompt you to connect an external service before its tools become available.
L764: In Codex CLI, enter `/plugins` to open the plugin browser. Install a plugin from a configured marketplace, then start a new session before using its bundled skills or tools.
L765: ### Use plugins from a supported surface
L766: 
L767: Plugins aren’t available in the IDE extension. To browse and install plugins for Codex, use the ChatGPT desktop app or Codex CLI.
L768: 
L769: Extend what ChatGPT and Codex can do, for example:
L770:   * Install the Codex Security plugin to scan authorized code and confirm plausible vulnerability findings.
L771:   * Install the Gmail plugin to work with Gmail.
L772:   * Install the Google Drive plugin to work across Drive, Docs, Sheets, and Slides.
L773:   * Install the Slack plugin to summarize channels or draft replies.
L774: 
L775: A plugin can contain one or more of these parts:
L776:   * Skills: reusable instructions for specific kinds of work. ChatGPT and Codex can load them when needed so they follow the right steps and use the right references or helper scripts for a task.
L777:   * Connectors: connections to tools like GitHub, Slack, or Google Drive, so ChatGPT and Codex can read information from those tools and take actions in them. Connectors expose tools and can optionally include custom UI.
L778:   * MCP servers: services that give ChatGPT and Codex access to more tools or shared information, often from systems outside your local project. They’re also the services behind connectors. They define tools, enforce auth, return structured data, and perform actions against external systems.
L779:   * Browser extensions: browser capabilities that a plugin needs for its workflow.
L780:   * Hooks: commands that run at configured lifecycle points. Review and trust plugin hooks before you enable them.
L781:   * Scheduled task templates: reusable starting points for recurring tasks where scheduled tasks are available.
L782: You can share plugins by publishing them through a marketplace source, such as a repo marketplace for a project or team. See cite415†Build plugins†developers.openai.com for marketplace setup, packaging, and distribution guidance.
L783: 
L784: If you are building an integration, start with cite416†Build an MCP server†developers.openai.com . If the plugin needs custom UI, use the cite417†optional UI guide†developers.openai.com .
L785: ## Use and install plugins
L786: ### Universal plugin directory
L787: 
L788: ChatGPT and Codex use the same public plugin catalog. To browse and install plugins from a supported graphical surface:
L789: 
L790:   * On the web, turn on Work in the switcher and open Plugins.
L791:   * In the ChatGPT desktop app, select ChatGPT and turn on Work in the switcher, or select Codex. Then open Plugins.
L792: 
L793: cite418†Image: Plugins Directory in the ChatGPT desktop app L794: 
L795: The Plugins Directory organizes plugins into tabs:
L796:   * OpenAI: plugins built by OpenAI.
L797:   * Your workspace name: plugins provided by your workspace.
L798:   * Personal: personal marketplace plugins, including Created by me and Shared with me sections when those plugins are available.
L799: 
L800: Use the separate Installed row to review plugins you already installed.
L801: ### Install and use a plugin
L802: 
L803: Once you open the Plugins Directory:
L804: 
L805:   1. Search or browse for a plugin, then open its details.
L806:   2. Select the plus button to install the plugin.
L807:   3. If the plugin needs a connector, connect it when prompted. Some plugins ask you to authenticate during install. Others wait until the first time you use them.
L808:   4. After installation, start a new chat and ask ChatGPT or Codex to use the plugin.
L809: ### Connect supported partners with Sign in with ChatGPT
L810: 
L811: Sign in with ChatGPT is rolling out in beta for supported plugins and partner sites, including Airtable, GitLab, HubSpot, Notion, Supabase, and Vercel. When the option is available, select Sign in with ChatGPT while connecting the plugin to create or link your account with that service.
L812: Signing in shares only your name, email address, and profile picture, when available, with the partner. It doesn’t grant the plugin access to your data or approve actions automatically. Review and approve the plugin’s requested permissions as a separate step before using the connection.
L813: 
L814: After you install a plugin, you can use it directly in the prompt window:
L815: 
L816: cite419†Image: Installed plugin on the Plugins page L817: 
L818: Describe the task directly
L819: Ask for the outcome you want, such as “Summarize unread Gmail threads from today” or “Pull the latest launch notes from Google Drive.”
L820: 
L821: Use this when you want ChatGPT to choose the right installed tools for the task.
L822: 
L823: Choose a specific plugin
L824: 
L825: Type `@` to invoke the plugin or one of its bundled skills explicitly.
L826: 
L827: Use this when you want to be specific about which plugin or skill ChatGPT should use. See cite230†Skills & Plugins .
L828: ### Plugin browser in Codex CLI
L829: 
L830: In Codex CLI, run the following command to open the plugin browser:
L831: 
L832:     `codex
L833:     /plugins`
L834: 
L835: cite420†Image: Plugins list in Codex CLI L836: 
L837: The CLI plugin browser groups plugins by marketplace. Use the marketplace tabs to switch sources, open a plugin to inspect details, install or uninstall marketplace entries, and press `Space` on an installed plugin to turn it on or off.
L838: ### API key availability
L839: 
L840: If you cite421†sign in to Codex with an OpenAI API key , you can browse, install, and manage supported OpenAI-curated plugins in Codex CLI and Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app. Some plugins aren’t available with API key authentication because their connection flows require unsupported OAuth capabilities. Review plugin usage on the cite422†Platform Usage page†platform.openai.com .

payload.message:
Two findings:

### HIGH — Codex hook command is POSIX-only, so Windows compaction reinjection does not launch

**File:** `hooks/hooks-codex.json:9`

**Conditions:** Codex runs natively on Windows and executes the fallback `command` because no `commandWindows` is supplied.

**Issue:** The command uses `"${PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/run-hook.cmd"`. `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` is POSIX-shell syntax; Windows `cmd.exe` requires `%PLUGIN_ROOT%`, while PowerShell requires `$env:PLUGIN_ROOT`. Codex explicitly supports a Windows-specific `commandWindows` override, but this entry omits it. The polyglot `.cmd` wrapper cannot help because the shell must first resolve and launch the wrapper.

**Impact:** The new hook is skipped/fails open after compaction on Windows, so the exact behavioral regression this change claims to fix remains there.

**Evidence:** The official Codex hook contract documents `commandWindows` as the Windows-only override and exposes `PLUGIN_ROOT` as an environment variable, not a manifest placeholder. The added tests run only under Bash and merely assert the POSIX command string at `tests/hooks/test-session-start-codex.sh:88-107`, so they endorse rather than catch the broken Windows path.

### MEDIUM — Tests never exercise the changed Codex lifecycle path

**File:** `tests/hooks/test-session-start-codex.sh:20-24, 36-58, 88-107`

**Conditions:** Hook discovery, trust handling, command execution, matcher dispatch, or model-context delivery differs from the test’s assumptions.

**Issue:** Every behavioral assertion pipes a hand-written payload directly into `bash "$HOOK_UNDER_TEST"`. The only config check parses JSON with Node. No test starts Codex with the packaged plugin, triggers or resumes after compaction, or inspects the model-visible prompt/context.

**Impact:** The suite can pass while Codex never discovers, trusts, launches, or injects the hook. It proves script text generation, not the changed Codex startup/compaction contract.

**Required coverage:** Add an isolated installed-plugin integration test using Codex with hook trust bypassed, trigger a real compact lifecycle, and assert `<CONTEXT_RESTORED>` appears in the immediate post-compaction model input. At minimum, execute the configured command through Codex rather than directly invoking the Bash script.

No files were modified.

payload.message:
CONFIRMED — HIGH

**Conditions:** Native Windows Codex executes the hook’s fallback `command` through PowerShell because `commandWindows` is absent.

**Evidence:**

- `hooks/hooks-codex.json:9` contains `"\"${PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/run-hook.cmd\" session-start-codex"` with no Windows override.
- Official Codex hooks documentation defines `commandWindows` specifically for Windows command syntax.
- A native PowerShell reproduction of the same quoted-executable pattern fails with `ParserError`; adding the call operator `&` succeeds.
- Repository history independently confirms the exact defect: commit `bc20cdaa556dcaea0a8b9b31f8ff5216376820ef` is titled `fix(codex): invoke Windows hook command through PowerShell` and adds precisely:
  `"commandWindows": "& \"${PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/run-hook.cmd\" session-start-codex"`.
  The reviewed rebuilt branch omitted that prior fix.
- `tests/hooks/test-session-start-codex.sh:88-107` only validates the POSIX `command` string and never requires or executes `commandWindows`.

**Rationale:** On native Windows the hook command fails before `run-hook.cmd` starts, so post-compaction bootstrap reinjection does not occur. This is a platform-specific functional failure of the change’s primary behavior.
